extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, media scholars, news editors and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for evaluating which foreign events are selected as news, using twelve news factors (frequency, threshold, unambiguity, etc.) and principles describing how those factors combine and operate in news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The time-span needed for an event to unfold and acquire meaning; events that fit the news organization's schedule (e.g., a murder fitting the daily cycle) are more reportable than gradual occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer events with short, clearly bounded time-spans that match publishing/airing cycles; gradual long-term trends are less likely to be selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The size or intensity of an event — events must pass an absolute threshold of magnitude/intensity to be reported, and larger events are more likely to be news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection favors events exceeding a perceived magnitude cutoff; the greater the intensity/size, the higher the probability of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: The clearer the meaning of an event, the more likely it is to be selected; clear implications make better copy than ambiguous events requiring complex context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose events whose causes and consequences are straightforward to explain; ambiguous events that need extensive contextualization are less newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural proximity and relevance to the audience increase newsworthiness — events with cultural relevance or that may affect the audience are preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize events that resonate with the audience's cultural frame or have concrete relevance to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Events fitting the journalist's pre-existing image or expectations are more likely to be selected; predictable events that match an outlet's mental map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is biased toward events that conform to established narratives, stereotypes, or editorial expectations (mental maps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Within meaningful and consonant events, the unexpected, rare, or surprising are more newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for deviations from routine or predictions — surprise increases news value, provided the event remains understandable and relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a story is defined as news, it will continue to be defined as such for some time, even if its absolute amplitude has been reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors keep following existing items (ongoing stories) to sustain coverage and audience familiarity; continuation can justify repeated coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are selected to form a balanced whole — editors balance coverage types and prioritize accordingly to fill the news bulletin or page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is influenced by the need to compose a coherent news package (geographic, topical, tonal balance), not solely by isolated event attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Elite Nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Events concerning powerful nations (e.g., US, UK) receive more attention than those concerning less influential nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geopolitical weight elevates news probability; occurrences in or involving elite nations are privileged in foreign news selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Elite People
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions of elite persons (politicians, celebrities) are more newsworthy than actions of ordinary people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prominence of actors increases selection likelihood; stories tied to elites attract coverage beyond similar events involving non-elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Events portrayed as the actions of individuals rather than as the result of impersonal social forces attract more coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame stories around individuals, human interest angles, and personal agency to increase news appeal; depersonalized structural explanations reduce immediate newsability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Bad news is more newsworthy than good news.' Negativity is often described as the basic news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative events (conflict, disaster, scandal) are inherently prioritized; editors are biased toward reporting undesirable or harmful occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additivity (core hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more factors an event satisfies, the higher the probability it becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess events by tallying satisfied news factors — cumulative presence increases selection likelihood; use as a heuristic for expected news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity (core hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one factor is strongly present, others may be less necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very strong presence of a single factor (e.g., extreme threshold or elite actor) can compensate for lack of other factors when predicting selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion (core hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events satisfying none or very few factors will not become news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the absence of most factors as a predictor of non-selection; marginal events with low scores on the factors tend to be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection (chain of communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage where events are chosen for coverage — the more factors an event satisfies, the more likely it is to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is guided by the twelve factors and the core hypotheses; it is the first gate in the chain from event to reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distortion (chain of communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once selected, the newsworthy factors are accentuated — coverage amplifies aspects that fit news criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that reporting will accentuate elements that increase perceived news value (personalization, negativity, elite reference), potentially skewing representation of the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication (chain of communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection and distortion are repeated at all stages from event to reader, propagating the prioritized aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that multiple actors (reporters, editors, wire services) reiterate and reinforce the same news-value-driven framing through the distribution process.
